name: PC Engine / TurboGrafx-16
description: A compact console co-developed by NEC and Hudson Soft, with an 8-bit CPU paired with 16-bit graphics hardware. It briefly outsold the Famicom in Japan, was sold in North America as the TurboGrafx-16, and became famous for shooters and arcade ports on credit-card-sized HuCards.
curiosities: HuCards are about the size of a credit card, and the Japanese PC Engine itself is only around 14 cm square.
The American TurboChips have their pin order reversed relative to Japanese HuCards, which acts as a crude region lock.
NEC's CD-ROM² add-on of 1988 was the first CD-ROM drive for a home video game console.
The HuC6280 is a modified 65C02 that includes the sound generator and a timer on the same die.
Hudson Soft designed it and NEC built it; it launched in Japan on 30 October 1987.
In Japan it outsold Sega's Mega Drive.
The TurboGrafx-16, its North American version of 1989, is a much larger console in a black case.
Its HuC6280 processor is 8-bit, at a fast 7.16 MHz; the 16 in TurboGrafx-16 stands for its 16-bit graphics chip.
With a single controller port it needs a multitap for more players; Bomberman supports five.
The PC Engine GT and TurboExpress are handhelds that play the same HuCards.
The SuperGrafx of 1989, a more powerful model, got only a handful of games of its own.
CD-ROM² games could play CD audio, so many had recorded soundtracks and voice acting.
story: NEC and Hudson Soft built the PC Engine around Hudson's own chips; it launched in Japan in October 1987 in a tiny box, its games on credit-card-sized HuCards.

In Japan it beat the Famicom for a while and, in 1988, became the first console with a CD-ROM add-on. In North America, as the TurboGrafx-16 of 1989, it lost to the Genesis and Super NES. Bonk, R-Type, Ys and many shooters made it beloved.
It sold millions of units in all its forms, and NEC brought back a PC Engine Mini in 2020.
